I started playing with Linux about ten years ago. I do believe I still have the install disc(s) for whatever the current version of Ubuntu was at the time as well as random Fedora and odd items like an old PuppyLinux Live CD. Would have to get CD spools out of storage to find.

The past few years I have been a real big fan of CrunchBang. I loved it, but switched back to Mint after development stopped for it. (Though I hear they have picked it up again). I'm a big fan of simple, light weight installs and desktops that just work. OpenBox and XFCE are my preferred desktops on any distro. New Gnome, Unity, KDE.. blah.

Right now I am rocking Mint on my desktop workstation. This is my work computer. On my laptop, straight Debian. Home media/backup/dev server: Debian. Raspberry Pis: Raspian... On all my virtual servers... Debian. I like Debian.
Because after 6 months of using Windows boot times start to reach 10 mins. Oh and I prefer bash over command.com or even worse powershell.

I wanted to use emacs, but couldn't find one that worked with DOS. I cleared a partition and installed slackware. Then it didn't take long until I deleted the DOS partition to get more room for Linux.

I wanted to get into programming, and Linux was the platform "serioznesses" programmers used. Got used to it, and now I only keep Windows for gaming. Recently switch back to Ubuntu though. Seems like the New Linux kernel doesn't play we'll with my network card in my laptop, and Ubuntu has been the only version I've seen fix it so far. I miss you Arch... :-(
I like to tinker around with software, I also am going into programming. I have tried dozens of distros until I decided on Arch, the packaging system is just so much easier in my opinion.
I bought a PC with Windoze ME....worst OS ever, I got so pissed of that I begged a copy of redhat from the sysadmin at my college. It's all good since.:-)

I started on Windows doing web development and quickly moved to Mac when OS X came out. Over time, that just became so restrictive and I couldn't get the versions of software I needed. I eventually moved to Ubuntu, after using Mephis for a couple of years, then to Crunchbang until it was shut down. I converted the apt sources to straight Debian and am now running on Jessie.

It's all OpenBox for me. I don't need lots of interface candy, I just want something that works.

On my laptop, which I use for basically anything, I use Debian, just because it is way more flexible + there seems to be some kind of issue with my graphics card that windows can't handle.

The best thing about Linux is the freedom I get, I can remove and place and edit whatever the hell I want, if the edited program fails, that is my problem. Also the ease of bash, it is delightful. Repositories filled with programs, and when you install a program, and you need additional programs/libraries for that particular program, it will just ask me whether I want that installed with it, the option to say no is just great(I know saying no is not good). Another great thing is the fact that drivers are basically there, no need to go on another pc, download ethernet controller drivers and download all the others too. And the stability of course.

On my desktop I use windows only to play steam games, if it wasn't for that, I would be using Linux on all my devices.

I also use some raspberry pis.

As a programmer, I found myself using Linux more and more as the platform for applications I was working on. Soon, it didn't make any sense to use Windows when all my work targetted Linux. Linux/posix/unix conventions are pretty much lingua franca in the programming world anyway. On top of all that, I've been bitten too many times by closed source bullshit that I couldn't fix, so I resolved to use as much open source software as possible. That rules out Mac OS as a "unixy" alternative. Therefore: Linux.

I wanted something light and free with all the source. And after package management, there is no going back. It takes seconds to get all the source and all thr build dependencies in Debian compared to hours or even days on Windows. With just one update system for everything installed and a trusted source to install from.

Then you can't not love Unix when you get it and learn the history. Or not love the shell.

Switching to ARM or MIPS devices is no big deal. As is being all 64bit.

After I left RISC OS, I was never happy on Windows, but I'm happier on Debain Testing then on any other OS. And have been for many years.

Broke my Win install, didn't have a Win CD on hand.

Never went back :D

Started dabbling back in 2003 or so, and wound up -wrecking- my machine at the time. Came crawling back to Windows for a few years, and then once things got a little more n00b-friendly I gave it another go back when Ubuntu didn't suck.

I now run Mint as my primary and occasionally go back to windows when the little lady wants to photoshop but that's about it.

I've been an acolyte for FOSS ever since.

I have been using Linux for almost 20 years, and Windows before that. I still use both, depending on the job. I started with Red Hat, moved to Mandrake, SuSE, Debian, and others, until Gentoo released in 2003. Been using that and Fedora since Fedora Core came out. Now I mainly use Fedora since I really don't have the time to tinker with Gentoo like I used to.

I use Linux for servers, some desktops, and anything that doesn't need specific games on it. I mostly use Windows to game on, but I also use Visual Studio for development. Linux has a great dev environment, and I use it too, but VS is superior to me.

Either way, I use both.

Most recently? Privacy concerns with Windows 10.

The first time it was because I had an old cheap laptop and the only way to get windows onto it was to dual boot Linux. As it turns out, Linux ran a little better.

The second time it was because I needed a certain kind of scripting environment.

Now with privacy dead, I'll probably stay Linux forever. Its already gotten to the point where it is easier for me to manage than Windows.
